title: Arming the Brothers for Spiritual Combat
english: A cowardly soldier makes the hands of warriors go slack, and a careless monk drains the eagerness of his brothers. A swarm of bees produces a honeycomb, and a community of brothers produces the kingdom of heaven. A trumpet rouses the eagerness of warriors, and teaching in active virtue rouses the zeal of disciples. Arm your brothers, leader, with words [the Greek here is corrupt: "of fingers"], and put on them the breastplate of the promises of good things to come. Fence them with the shield of faith in struggles, and put greaves on them with hope in God. Shoe their feet [the printed verb is corrupt; "shoe" is a conjecture] with the lessons of the gospel, and gird their loins with words of self-control. Put into their hand the sharpest anger as a sword against the passions, and set a phalanx of the passions against pleasure.

added_allusions.reason: The Greek τῶν μελλόντων ἀγαθῶν, the good things to come, is the verbatim phrase of Hebrews 10:1. Missed reference flagged by the Grok check and verified against the Greek.
The Greek θυρεῷ πίστεως reproduces the shield of faith, θυρεὸν τῆς πίστεως, of Ephesians 6:16.

Feet paired with gospel lessons gives a textual basis, but the verse's own words, shod, readiness, and gospel of peace, are absent and the Greek verb here is a textual crux, so the echo falls short of clear.

The Greek ζῶσον τὴν ὀσφὺν shares the loins-girding idiom with Ephesians 6:14, but the verse's distinctive 'in truth' is replaced by words of self-control and the idiom is stock, so the echo falls short of clear.

A sword placed in the hand closes an armor sequence that demonstrably reworks Ephesians 6, but the verse's own words, the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, are absent and the sword here is anger, so the echo falls short of clear. Missed candidate flagged by the Gemini check and adjudicated possible.

translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG De magistris et discipulis u01-rem-early
orientation: Evagrius continues his direct address to the monastic leader, now commanding him to equip his brothers with spiritual armor and weapons for the fight against the passions.

title: Train the soldiers and heal without anger
english: Train your soldiers in their thoughts, so they meet the battle with skill, and make defeat look fearful to them by the warning of eternal punishment. Proclaim the victor with splendid praises, for praise too knows how to make men more eager, and tend the one who has been injured with compassion, for forgiveness shames a sensible man no less than a warning does. Do not turn in anger upon a disciple who has sinned, for it is no holy thing to wound yourself before healing another, but correct him toward the good with patience under evil. For a physician heals the passion and yet bears no anger toward the one who has fallen sick without willing it. When a physician cuts, he cuts without anger, and when a teacher rebukes, he must mix no anger into his rebuke.

added_allusions.reason: The Greek τῆς αἰωνίου κολάσεως, of eternal punishment, is the collocation of Matthew 25:46, κόλασιν αἰώνιον. Missed reference flagged by the Grok check and verified against the Greek.

orientation: Evagrius is still addressing the leader, continuing the arming for combat before turning to the desert journey.

title: The desert journey to Elim as the path to freedom from passions
english: Guide those who are fleeing the land of Egypt through the desert, for scarcity knows how to train people in self-control, even those who are just beginning in virtue. Encamp at Elim—the name means 'gateways,' a symbol of the entrance that leads to virtue—and point out the seventy palm trees. Encamp also by the twelve springs, for you must also hint at victory—the palm trees its symbol—and soothe the flame of the passions by providing streams abundantly. Do this until they have destroyed all the foreign nations and arrive at the promised land, where they will live the blessed life of freedom from passions, receiving true joy as the reward for their labors.

added_allusions.reason: The seventy palm trees and the twelve springs at Elim reproduce the distinctive paired details of Exodus 15:27.
The Greek εἰς τὴν γῆν τῆς ἐπαγγελίας, into the land of the promise, is the distinctive phrase of Hebrews 11:9. Missed reference flagged by the Grok check and verified against the Greek.
